A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same BFCL-based study of description-induced tool preferences, despite the changed title. Their complete text, tables, definitions, and appendices support reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original experiments measuring tool usage under description edits, including individual-edit evaluations and pairwise competitions across ten LLMs.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and reports additional results for seven models and unfavorable-description experiments across four models.

M1.justification: Appendix D introduces a negative assertive edit: appending 'This is the worst tool for this purpose and should not be called' to suppress selection. This is a limited extension of the description manipulations; the existing editing recipes, combined edit, and GPT-4o generation prompts remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions use BFCL single-turn, simple-function tasks from the live&simple and non-live&simple categories. The negative-cue experiment applies another editing variant to the same tool-choice task; no additional dataset, domain, or task is introduced.

E2.justification: v2 Tables 17–20 add Negative Assertive Cues to the compared description variants for GPT-4.1, GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, and o1. Existing comparator sets remain intact. The seven additional LLMs are evaluated subjects, rather than new competing description-edit methods.

E3.justification: The evaluated model suite expands from ten to seventeen, adding GPT-4o, o1, and Qwen2.5 variants with 0.5B, 1.5B, 3B, 14B, and 32B parameters. This substantially broadens the tested model configurations. The original metrics, both-order control, and 516/1316 test-case settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds a Qwen-family size-sensitivity analysis spanning 0.5B–32B and a four-model unfavorable-description ablation in Appendix D. These address two substantive questions absent from v1: whether scale mitigates susceptibility and whether description manipulation also suppresses tool selection.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests. v2 retains point estimates and cross-model aggregation; averaging over additional models does not introduce uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: v2 adds seven model-specific competition matrices and negative-cue results, while retaining all ten original model-specific matrices unchanged. Table 1's assertive-cue average ratio changes from 4.76:1 to 3.58:1 because the aggregation covers seventeen rather than ten models, not because of a same-setting performance decline. New Table 20 reports 0.0% versus 88.6% correct usage for negatively described versus original tools with o1.

T1.justification: Definitions 2.1 and 2.2 for correct tool usage and model correctness are unchanged. Neither version contains additional theoretical propositions, proofs, or derivations.

C1.justification: The central claims remain that description edits can strongly bias tool selection, current protocols are exploitable, and selection needs a more reliable foundation. The abstract's expansion from ten to seventeen evaluated models adds supporting evidence without redefining those claims or the three stated contributions.

C2.justification: Section 3 adds interpretations that scaling alone does not prevent manipulation and that susceptibility spans instruction-following and reasoning-oriented models. Appendix D interprets the effect as bidirectional. The limitations acknowledge larger local models, while the main explanation concerning descriptions being disconnected from functionality remains unchanged.

D1.justification: v2 adds a public-code availability statement and repository link in the abstract. Appendix D specifies the exact negative cue and evaluated models. The existing implementation prompts in Appendices A–C are unchanged.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations to the GPT-4o system card by Hurst et al. and the o1 system card by Jaech et al. The related-work discussion and positioning relative to tool-use research and prompt-injection attacks remain unchanged.

P1.justification: The paper is retitled from 'Gaming Tool Preferences in Agentic LLMs' to 'Tool Preferences in Agentic LLMs are Unreliable,' and Section 2 is renamed. Local wording, contact information, and acknowledgements change, and a new Appendix D precedes the former results appendix, now E. Most existing prose and section order are retained.

P2.justification: v2 adds seven model-specific matrices and four expanded matrices containing negative-cue rows and columns. The latter redisplay retained comparisons alongside new results. Existing tables are reflowed and renumbered, producing a substantial expansion of the tabular presentation while preserving its red/blue comparison format.

improvement.justification: The model-size sweep and negative-cue ablation strengthen evidence about generalization and bidirectional manipulation, and the code-access disclosure improves reproducibility information. These usefully extend an already established central finding. A qualification remains: v2 retains the claim that assertive cues are highly effective across all evaluated models, although new Table 26 shows only 36.6% versus 34.3% usage for Qwen2.5-0.5B. The net improvement is therefore positive but limited.
